items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up. The call went from 'Hello, this is [Rance] with [Einstein] moving. How can I help you?' straight into spelling out a last name.
No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' — no roadmap, no timeframe, no confirmation. The customer never knew what the next thirteen minutes would contain.

Move date was never actually confirmed, and there is a live date error in the record. The customer said 'can we do maybe like the 13th of October' and Rance's next line is 'October 6th.' There is no correction anywhere afterward — he moved straight to 'Cool, yeah work on that' and then to the origin address. Whatever date is sitting in EMMA behind this estimate, the customer believes it is October 13th and the transcript says Rance said the 6th. Availability was never checked for either date.
Special considerations never probed — no long walks, narrow hallways, tight turns, low ceilings, at either end.

Packing needs were never asked. The customer raised packing himself at the very end of the call ('do you put things in the boxes or just take the boxes?'), and Rance's answer was excellent — but it arrived after the estimate was already built and after the customer had declined to book, so it could not be used to build value or size the job.

Storage stops and additional stops never asked. On an Austin-to-San-Antonio move where the customer has no destination lined up yet, a storage stop is not a hypothetical — it is a realistic outcome, and it would change the price structure entirely.
Walk distance never asked at either end.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used to make five hours and $1,305 concrete.

No Worries Damage Coverage was mis-branded as 'free evaluation coverage.' The substance was strong and actually went beyond the rubric — '$2,000 per move to repair replace or reimburse... That's not only gonna cover the furniture that we're moving, but also the residence as well. So if there's any stuff on the walls floors anything like that' — but the brand name never landed and the 60c/lb industry baseline was never given, so the customer has no yardstick for how unusual $2,000 with no deductible actually is.

The Save Your Ass speech was two-thirds delivered and then abandoned. He landed the framing and the examples — 'one of the biggest ones you can control. Is how well prepared you are... like lamps, hang those, hang photos, like any of that kind of stuff that it's just gonna require a more prep work and smaller trips to and from the truck. So, the better you consolidating everything in the boxes force wicker more efficient can be on your move and more money we can save you' — but there was no 'take a carload' tip and no sense-check close. He moved straight on with 'But yeah, as far as the pricing and everything that's the way it goes,' which is the verbal equivalent of shrugging off the point he just made.

No deposit required was never mentioned. This is the highest-cost miss on the call. The customer explicitly deferred — 'if you can just send me the estimate for now until I get like my address I'll, I'm just gonna wait to officially do it' — and the exact counter to 'I'll wait' is 'booking costs you nothing, holds your date, and you can change it free once you have the address.' It was never said.

No booking-friction removal of any kind on a customer who told Rance the price was right. 'I think the pricing is good like this is kind of around where I was looking for' is a buying signal, and it drew 'Yes sir. Sounds good.' No attempt to hold the date, no 'what would you need to know to be comfortable booking today?', no specific follow-up commitment or callback date.

No bolded-details framing on the outgoing estimate and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. 'Reply back to that email' was offered as a way to book later, not as a way to verify that the details — including the disputed move date — are right. On a quote built from a placeholder destination address the customer invented on the spot, the verification ask was the most important line in the call and it never happened.

Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' The customer had to interrupt his own goodbye to ask the packing question — 'Alright, sounds great. Thank you. Well actually I have one more question.'
No hours and no direct contact number given — just 'you can give us a call back.'

Customer's name used zero times. Rance had him spell out both first and last name ('four FA, W. A. Z.' and 'A-L-J-E-S-H-I'), confirmed the spelling back, and then never once used it in thirteen minutes. 'Yes sir' carried the whole call.
No storage referral offered to a customer who said outright he is moving to San Antonio without a place lined up — the clearest Sparefoot trigger in the sample.
top_strength: Rance's pricing block is the most complete in this week's sample and his estimate is built the way the accuracy rock wants it built. In one uninterrupted pass he delivered nine of the ten Section 3 bullets: the super-simple opener, the rate framed correctly per mover per hour ('$104 per mover per hour. We would send out two movers for your particular move. So you'd be looking at $208 an hour'), the full inclusions list, disassembly and reassembly with a nice specific ('for a one bedroom apartment that's pretty much just the bed'), the full no-hidden-fees run, the $265 trip fee named and explained rather than buried, damage coverage extended to the residence itself, Meet Your Mover ('a couple of days before your move we'll send you an email that introduce you to the guys are going to be taking care of it, so you don't just have random [strangers] showing up at the front door'), and the On-Time Guarantee with the reason attached ('we're gonna start immediately discounting money of your final bill. So there's no [stress] around a move. They wonder where your movers are'). Section 4 is a clean 4/4 with the sense-check. The estimate itself is disciplined: 'Typically a one bedroom apartment is gonna take two movers about two and a half to three and a half hours to complete yours. I'm gonna put it right at three hours, probably right there in the middle' — a stated range and a mid-range landing, not a pad — and then the intercity variable handled honestly and specifically: 'it's probably closer to a two hour drive to San antonio on our trucks. They don't get quite as fast as the passenger vehicle.' He also front-loaded the lead record properly, capturing name spelling, phone and email inside the first ninety seconds, which is exactly the failure mode that sank the reference call last week. And when the customer finally asked about packing, the answer was the best single stretch of the call — full-service or room-by-room, priced at the same hourly rate, supplies brought out and 'we only charge you for what we actually use on the job,' with concrete anchors of roughly three hours and about $189 in materials for a one-bedroom, caveated as an average.
coaching_note: Rance did the expensive work well and then gave away the close. The customer's own words were 'I think the pricing is good like this is kind of around where I was looking for' — that is a qualified buyer telling you the number lands — and the only thing standing between him and a booking was that he does not have a San Antonio address yet. That is not a real objection, and there is a one-line answer to it that was never said: 'Totally get it. Here's the thing though — there's no deposit and no card on file to book, and moving the date or updating the address once you sign a lease costs you nothing. So I can hold October thirteenth for you right now, and the only thing that changes when you get your address is I update the destination and re-send. Want me to lock it in so the date is yours?' That single move converts 'send me the estimate' into a booking at zero risk to the customer, and it also solves the second problem on this call, which is that Rance has no follow-up mechanism at all — no callback date, no check-in commitment, nothing but 'reply to the email whichever wants more convenient for you.' Fix the date before anything else, though, because there is a hard error in the record. The customer said the thirteenth of October; Rance's next line was 'October 6th' and nobody corrected it. Pull this record today and confirm which date the estimate was actually built against — if the email went out with the sixth on it, the customer is going to open it, see a date he never asked for, and quietly go elsewhere. That is also a Section 7 lesson worth teaching generally: the 'reply with any corrections' line exists precisely to catch this, and Rance used the reply-to-email as a booking channel instead of a verification ask. Third, finish the Save Your Ass speech. He got the framing right and the examples right and then stopped one beat short of both the carload tip and the sense-check. The customer is moving from an 825 sqft first-floor apartment where you can park right out front — the carload line is easy money: 'And anything small and awkward — lamps, the pictures off the walls, the bins on the balcony — throw those in your own car before we get there. On a move with a two-hour drive in it, every loose item we don't handle twice is real money. Does that make sense?' Fourth, and this is the smallest fix with the biggest presence payoff: he made the customer spell out Fawaz Aljeshi letter by letter, read it back to confirm, and then never used the name once in thirteen minutes. Two uses in the pricing block and one at the close would move this call up a full point on phone presence by itself. Two business notes for Amanda rather than for Rance. One: this customer is moving to San Antonio with no lease signed, which is the clearest storage-referral trigger we have seen in the sample and it went unoffered — worth checking whether reps even know Sparefoot is a card they can play. Two: no estimate-accuracy padding flag on this call, which is the good news — he stated two and a half to three and a half and landed at three. The accuracy risk here is different and worth tracking separately: the whole quote is built on a destination address the customer made up on the spot ('you can put in 111 Pro. Bandi... Street'), with the floor, the walk and the access all unknown, and Rance correctly flagged that out loud ('I don't know what floor or anything it's on yet so it could change a little bit'). If this one books, it needs a re-quote before move day, not just a date change.
phone_presence_notes: Relaxed, unhurried and never pushy — he gave generous, thorough answers and let the customer take his time — but the warmth is almost entirely carried by the word 'Cool,' which appears roughly a dozen times as his only acknowledgment token, alongside 'Yes sir'; the customer's name is used zero times despite being spelled out and confirmed, the stressor question was asked and then not engaged with when answered, and the long pricing and estimate blocks reduce the customer to 'Uh-huh.'
audio_review_reason: The transcript gives almost no signal either way on warmth — 'Cool' a dozen times and 'Yes sir' can read as genuinely easygoing or as disengaged monotone, and nothing else in the language separates the two, which is exactly the ambiguity the flagging rule is for. Audio would also settle the material question on this call: whether Rance actually said 'October 6th' after the customer asked for the thirteenth, or whether that is a transcription error on a correctly heard date. That single word determines whether there is a live data error to fix in EMMA before the estimate email lands.
